quotes: Actinobacteria , Proteobacteria , and Verrucomicrobia were significantly enriched in diseased subjects, while Bacteroidetes and Cyanobacteria were significantly decreased; also, members of the Firmicutes were decreased; however, there was no significant difference in distribution between the PD and HC groups ( P > 0.05).
The microbiota of PD patients was characterized by significantly higher levels of several genera, such as Akkermansia , Escherichia , Bifidobacterium , Streptococcus , Clostridium , and Serratia.
note: PD patients compared to healthy controls.

title: Gut microbiome of treatment-naïve MS patients of different ethnicities early in disease course.
arms: Multiple sclerosis patients vs ethnicity-matched healthy controls
quotes: In all three ethnic groups, there was an increased relative abundance of the same single genus, Clostridium , compared to ethnicity-matched controls.
All three MS ethnic groups had an increase in the relative abundances of Clostridia species compared with their respective ethnicity-matched controls (Fig. 2 ).
note: MS patients vs ethnicity-matched healthy controls across three ethnic groups.

title: Hemorrhagic transformation in patients with large-artery atherosclerotic stroke is associated with the gut microbiota and lipopolysaccharide
arms: Stroke with hemorrhagic transformation vs healthy controls (also compares HT vs non-HT stroke subgroups)
quotes: Compared to the HC group, increased abundance of the phylum Proteobacteria ( P = 0.015) and decreased abundances of the phyla Bacteroidota ( P = 0.021) and Actinobacteriota ( P = 0.024) were detected in the HT group ( Additional Figure 1B ).

The three largest phyla in the healthy control, HT, and non-HT groups were Firmicutes , Proteobacteria , and Bacteroidetes , while Pseudomonadaceae , Lachnospiraceae , and Enterobacteriaceae were the most abundant families ( Figure 2 D and Additional Figure 1B ).
note: Hemorrhagic transformation vs healthy controls with within-stroke subgroup comparison.

title: Microbial dysbiosis and lack of SCFA production in a Spanish cohort of patients with multiple sclerosis.
arms: Multiple sclerosis patients vs healthy controls
quotes: Results Our results revealed an increment in the phylum Proteobacteria, especially the family Enterobacteriaceae, a lack in total SCFA excretion, and an altered profile of SCFAs in a Spanish cohort of MS patients.

No statistical differences between patients' and controls' microbiota could be observed at this taxonomical level; however, the tendency for the Proteobacteria phylum to increase in patients is remarkable.
note: MS patients vs healthy controls in Spanish cohort.

title: Orthopedic Surgery Causes Gut Microbiome Dysbiosis and Intestinal Barrier Dysfunction in Prodromal Alzheimer Disease Patients
arms: Normal cognition vs prodromal Alzheimer disease (SCD and aMCI subgroups)
quotes: Preoperative pAD-associated Bacterial Composition Before surgery, the NC group had the highest relative abundance of the phylum Firmicutes (median=53.63%) in contrast to that in the SCD (median=47.66%) and aMCI (median=50.60%) group.

Postoperative Changes of Bacteria Within Each Group The phylum Firmicutes remained stable in the NC group across all time points but gradually decreased over time in the aMCI group and decreased to the lowest level (median=37.04%) in the SCD group on postoperative day 3.
note: Normal cognition vs prodromal AD with disease severity subgroups, tracked postoperatively.

title: The Gut Microbiome in Parkinson's Disease: A Longitudinal Study of the Impacts on Disease Progression and the Use of Device-Assisted Therapies.
arms: Parkinson's disease vs healthy controls (longitudinal with device-assisted therapy subgroups)
quotes: When comparing PD with HC, we observed a persistent underrepresentation of the genera Butyricicoccus, Fusicatenibacter, Lachnospiraceae ND3007 group and Erysipelotrichaceae UCG-003 , as well as an overrepresentation of Lactobacillaceae and underrepresentation of Butyricicaceae at the family level across all three-time intervals, signifying a persistently altered GM in PD patients.

Within the DBS cohort, a persistent over representation of Prevotella was noted over both 6 and 12 months timepoints following DBS initiation, whilst the LCIG cohort did not show a clearly persistent taxa change across both 6 and 12 months intervals.
note: PD vs HC across time intervals with DBS vs LCIG device therapy subgroups.

title: Distinct responsiveness to rifaximin in patients with hepatic encephalopathy depends on functional gut microbial species
arms: Cirrhosis/hepatic encephalopathy vs healthy controls (with severity and treatment subgroups)
quotes: Streptococcus was enriched in the microbial populations of the compensated and decompensated cirrhosis groups (Figure [Link] , [Link] ).

Conversely, Streptococcus, Lactobacillus, and Bifidobacterium were not significantly abundant in the samples from patients with decompensated cirrhosis who did not receive PPI or lactulose treatment when compared with those from healthy controls or the compensated cirrhosis group following LEfSe analysis (Figure S1D , E ).
note: Cirrhosis/HE vs healthy controls with disease severity and treatment response subgroups.

title: Cross-Sectional Study on the Gut Microbiome of Parkinson's Disease Patients in Central China.
arms: Parkinson's disease patients vs healthy controls
quotes: Two phyla that were present in small proportions, namely, Actinobacteria (PD was 1.54% ± 2.11%, SP was 0.56% ± 0.77%, Mann–Whitney U test, p = 0.01) and Synergistetes (PD was 2.52% ± 7.26%, SP was 0.33% ± 1.12%, Mann–Whitney U test, p = 0.01), exhibited significant differences, and the abundance in the PD group was significantly increased.
In addition, we found that Bacteroides were enriched in the control group.
note: PD patients in Central China compared to healthy control group.

title: The ketogenic diet influences taxonomic and functional composition of the gut microbiota in children with severe epilepsy
arms: Children with severe epilepsy on ketogenic diet vs healthy control parents
quotes: Analysis of taxonomic changes in the gut microbiota during KD Dominant phyla in fecal samples from patients and controls at time point one were Firmicutes, Bacteroidetes, and Actinobacteria (Fig 2c), which are typically found in the human gut.
The relative abundance of the genus Bifidobacterium was significantly decreased in patients after 3 months on KD.
note: Ketogenic diet intervention in epileptic children vs healthy control parents at two time points.

title: Aging Gut-Brain Interactions: Pro-Inflammatory Gut Bacteria Are Elevated in Fecal Samples from Individuals Living with Alzheimer's Dementia.
arms: Alzheimer's dementia patients vs healthy controls
quotes: Taxonomic profiling at the phylum level showed a lower abundance of Bacteroidota (Bacteroidetes) and an increased abundance of Pseudomonadota (Proteobacteria) in the AD groups compared to the controls ( Figure 5 A), although neither of these changes were statistically significant.

In contrast, the control group had significantly higher levels of Bacteroides, Blautia, Roseburia , and Faecalibacterium genera ( p = 0.002, p = 0.02, p = 0.0001, p = 0.02 respectively) than the AD group.
note: Alzheimer's dementia patients vs healthy controls.

title: Gut microbiome changes in anti-N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor encephalitis patients.
arms: Anti-NMDAR encephalitis patients vs healthy controls
quotes: ASV analysis showed that Prevotella was significantly increased, while Bacteroides was reduced in the gut microbiota of the patients, compared with the controls.

The taxonomic results showed that the genus Prevotella was significantly increased (13.21% vs. 5.36%, P =0.048, by Wilcoxon test) and Bacteroides was considerably reduced (27.31% vs. 42.53%, P =0.024, by Wilcoxon test) in the patients compared to the controls (shown in Fig. 1 A).
note: Anti-NMDAR encephalitis patients vs healthy controls.

title: Specific gut microbiota alterations in essential tremor and its difference from Parkinson's disease.
arms: Essential tremor patients vs normal controls
quotes: Compared with NC, 7 genera were significantly reduced in ET, 4 of which ( Ruminococcus, Romboutsia, Mucispirillum, and Aeromonas ) were identified to be distinctive with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.705.

Compared to PD, 26 genera were found significantly different from ET, 4 of which ( Bacteroides , Fusobacterium , Phascolarctobacterium, and Lachnospira) were found distinguishable with an AUC of 0.756.
note: Essential tremor vs healthy controls; secondary comparison with Parkinson's disease.

title: Patients with Infections of The Central Nervous System Have Lowered Gut Microbiota Alpha Diversity
arms: Neuroinfection patients (viral and bacterial) vs healthy controls
quotes: Bacterial taxa such as Clostridium , Anaerostipes , Lachnobacterium , Lachnospira , and Roseburia were decreased in patients with neuroinfection when compared to controls.

Moreover, bacterial meningitis had a significantly higher abundance of Actinomycetota ( p = 0.037) compared to controls, whereas Verrucomicrobiota ( p = 0.03) was more abundant in viral cases than in healthy subjects ( Table 2 ).
note: Patients with CNS infections vs healthy controls; includes viral and bacterial etiology.

title: Metagenomics of the Gut Microbiome in Parkinson's Disease: Prodromal Changes.
arms: Parkinson's disease and prodromal subjects vs healthy controls
quotes: In feature-wise models adjusted for sequencing batch, age, pack-years smoking, BMI, and MED diet adherence, we observed significantly reduced abundance of several bacterial species, including Roseburia faecis , Eubacterium rectale , and E. ramulus (known for flavonoid degradation[ 66 ], as well as Oscillibacter_sp_57_20 , Bacteroides xylanisolvens , and E. siraeum in PD samples compared to healthy controls ( Fig. 3A ).

Similarly, we observed increased abundance of Bifidobacterium dentium and B. longum, which is consistent with prior reports of increased Bifidobacteria in PD [ 10 , 13 , 15 , 18 , 22 , 26 , 31 – 33 ].
note: PD and prodromal subjects vs healthy controls.

title: Multi-omics analyses identify gut microbiota-fecal metabolites-brain-cognition pathways in the Alzheimer's disease continuum.
arms: Healthy controls vs mild cognitive impairment vs Alzheimer's disease
quotes: Results There were significant group differences in gut microbial composition, which were driven by 8 microbial taxa (e.g., Staphylococcus and Bacillus) exhibiting a progressive increase in relative abundance from HC to MCI to AD, and 2 taxa (e.g., Anaerostipes) showing a gradual decrease.

Gut microbiomics analysis in AD, MCI and HC revealed no significant difference in alpha diversity among three groups, while there were significant group differences in gut microbial composition, which were driven by 8 microbial taxa exhibiting a progressive increase (e.g., Staphylococcus and Bacillus) in relative abundance from HC to MCI to AD, and 2 taxa (e.g., Anaerostipes) showing a gradual decrease.
note: Progressive disease stages from healthy controls through MCI to Alzheimer's disease.

title: Gut microbiome alterations in preclinical Alzheimer's disease
arms: Amyloid-positive cognitively normal (preclinical AD) vs amyloid-negative cognitively normal
quotes: The GLM analysis revealed that the genera Megamonas, Serratia, Leptotrichia and Clostridium (family Clostridiaceae) were increased in the Aβ+ CN group compared to the Aβ− CN group, whereas the genera CF231, Victivallis, Enterococcus, Mitsuokella and Clostridium (family Erysipelotrichaceae) were decreased in Aβ+ CN (Table 2 and Fig 1) In the ROC analysis, the logistic regression model with variables representing the presence or absence of each of the nine genera effectively distinguish Aβ+ and Aβ− CN with the AUC value of 0.

Among the four genera that were increased in the Aβ+ CN group, i. e., Megamonas, Serratia, Leptotrichia, and Clostridium (family Clostridiaceae), Megamonas was previously linked to Pre-DM [30], gestational DM [31], and obesity [32].
note: Amyloid-positive vs amyloid-negative cognitively normal subjects; represents preclinical Alzheimer's.

title: Altered Gut Microbial Metabolites in Amnestic Mild Cognitive Impairment and Alzheimer's Disease: Signals in Host-Microbe Interplay.
arms: Healthy controls vs amnestic mild cognitive impairment vs Alzheimer's disease
quotes: As shown in Figure S5 , Clostridia , with the capability of producing SCFAs like acetate, proprionate, butyratem and its phylum Firmicutes as well as the Clostridiales , Ruminococcaceae , Ruminococcus at order, family and genus levels, were significantly decreased in AD patients compared with aMCI or HC, while the propionate-producing Bacteroides was increased in aMCI patients compared with AD and HC ( Figure S5 ).

The consistent results of SCFA-producing bacteria and fecal SCFA concentration suggested that the decreased clusters of bacteria in Firmicutes, Clostridia , and Clostridiales of AD patients might contribute to the reduction of SCFAs.
note: Comparison across AD continuum: healthy controls, aMCI, and AD.

title: Association between the relative abundance of butyrate-producing and mucin-degrading taxa and Parkinson's disease.
arms: Parkinson's disease patients vs healthy controls
quotes: Beta-diversity was found to differ significantly between cases and controls, with depletion in the relative abundance of Faecalibacterium, Roseburia, Dorea, and Veillonella, and enrichment of the relative abundance of Akkermansia and Victivallis.
Our study found a reduction in butyrate-producing bacteria (e.g. Faecalibacterium and Roseburia) and an increase in mucin-degrading bacteria (Akkermansia) in PD cases compared to controls.
note: PD patients vs healthy controls.

title: Difference in gut microbial dysbiotic patterns between body-first and brain-first Parkinson's disease.
arms: Body-first Parkinson's disease vs brain-first Parkinson's disease
quotes: The gut microbiome in body-first PD showed a distinct profile, characterized by an increased presence of Escherichia coli and Akkermansia muciniphila, and a decreased abundance of short-chain fatty acid-producing commensal bacteria.
note: Compares microbiota profiles of body-first vs brain-first PD subtypes.

title: Alterations in nasal microbiota of patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
arms: ALS patients vs healthy controls
quotes: The nasal microbiome of ALS patients showed lower alpha diversity than that of corresponding healthy family members Genera Gaiella, Sphingomonas, Polaribacter_1, Lachnospiraceae_NK4A136_group, Klebsiella, and Alistipes were differentially enriched in ALS patients compared to controls.

Nasal microbiota composition in ALS patients significantly differed from that in healthy subjects (unweighted UniFrac P = 0 001), while Linear discriminant analysis Effect Size (LEfSe) analysis indicated that Bacteroidetes and Firmicutes dominated healthy nasal communities at the phylum level, whereas Actinobacteria was the predominant phylum and Thermoleophilia was the predominant class in ALS patients.
note: Clear HC comparison with nasal sampling

title: Changes in intestinal microbiota of HBV-associated liver cirrhosis with/without hepatic encephalopathy
arms: HBV-LC patients vs healthy controls; with/without hepatic encephalopathy subgroups
quotes: Difference in bacterial relative abundance between HBV-LC and control groups In the HBV-LC group, the abundance of the following significantly increased: Bacteroidia (37.95 ± 20.19 vs 23.52 ± 16.31, P = .049) at the class level; Streptococcaceae (5.60 ± 9.07 vs 0.81 ± 1.30, P = .035) at the family level
Our results show that the relative abundance of Pasteurellaceae and Pasteurellales in the stool of patients with HBV-LC increased significantly.
note: Main HC comparison plus within-disease HE/non-HE subgroups

title: Effect of Parkinson's disease and related medications on the composition of the fecal bacterial microbiota.
arms: PD patients vs healthy controls; treatment/clinical subgroups within PD
quotes: PD patients treated with L-dopa showed significantly higher relative abundances of Enterococcaceae , Clostridiales family XI, and the genera Peptoniphilus and Finegoldia , while Faecalibacterium and the Ruminococcus gauvreauii group were significantly decreased when compared to the controls.

PD patients with a hypokinetic-rigid (HR) phenotype showed a significantly increased relative abundance of Peptoniphilus and decreased relative abundance of Faecalibacterium compared to the control group
note: Main HC comparison plus multiple clinical subgroups (medications, phenotypes)

title: Gut Microbiota and Neurovascular Patterns in Amnestic Mild Cognitive Impairment.
arms: aMCI patients vs healthy controls
quotes: Several ASVs associated with aMCI participants are members of bacterial species known to be pro-inflammatory or have previously been associated with cognitive impairment, such as Bilophila (identified via all methods of differential abundance) and Faecalibacterium (identified via Random Forest analysis).

Bacteria associated with a healthy GMB, including Akkermansia (identified via MaAsLin2 analysis) and Turicibacter (identified via Random Forest and MaAsLin2 analysis), were more abundant in controls ( Figure 2 A,B).
note: Clear HC comparison between aMCI and controls

title: Gut microbiota composition reflects disease progression, severity and outcome, and dysfunctional immune responses in patients with hypertensive intracerebral hemorrhage
arms: ICH patients vs healthy controls; SAP/non-SAP subgroups
quotes: We observed that the relative abundances of Prevotella and Faecalibacterium were higher in the HC group than those in the ICH group, while the relative abundances of Enterococcus , Parabacteroides , Lachnoclostridium , Acidaminococcus , and Streptococcus were higher in the ICH group than those in the HC group.
Enterococcus enrichment and Prevotella depletion were also noted in the SAP group in contrast to the non-SAP group.
note: Main HC comparison plus within-disease SAP/non-SAP subgroups

title: Hypercoagulable state and gut microbiota dysbiosis as predictors of poor functional outcomes in acute ischemic stroke patients
arms: AIS patients vs healthy controls; hypercoagulable vs normal coagulation subgroups
quotes: LEfSe analysis showed that Parabacteroides , Oscillospira , Morganella , Megasphaera , and Alistipes were significantly enriched in AIS patients, whereas Prevotella , Roseburia , Faecalibacterium , and Blautia were significantly enriched in healthy controls ( Fig. 3E ).
AIS patients with hypercoagulable state had increased Alistipes abundance and decreased Prevotella abundance.
note: Main HC comparison plus within-disease coagulation status subgroups

title: Microbiome signatures of virulence in the oral-gut-brain axis influence Parkinson's disease and cognitive decline pathophysiology.
arms: PD/PDD patients vs healthy controls; PD-MCI/PDD disease subgroups
quotes: Several studies consistently indicated an increased abundance in Akkermansia, Bfidobacterium and Lactobacillus , and a depletion in butyrate producers such as Roseburia, Faecalibacterium and Blautia in PD patients.
The first genera cluster showed the enrichment of species for Bifidobacterium longum, Bilophila wadsworthia, Ruthenibacterium lactatiformans in PD-MCI patients (Figure S1D).
note: HC comparison with both oral and gut microbiota; multiple disease subgroups

title: Plasma exosomal miRNA expression and gut microbiota dysbiosis are associated with cognitive impairment in Alzheimer's disease.
arms: AD patients vs healthy controls
quotes: The findings revealed that the abundance of bacteria belonging to the family Propionibacteriaceae , as well as the genera Peptoniphilus , Anaerococcus, Tannerella , Arachnia , and Dermabacter , and the species Burkholderia cepacia , Fusobacterium necrophorum , Blautia hydrogenotrophica , Streptococcus porcinus , Streptococcus parasuis , and Actinomyces sp. oral taxon 848 , were significantly enriched in AD patients.

Conversely, the abundance of Romboutsia , Faecalibacterium , Roseburia , Sarcina at the genus level, as well as Massilistercora timonensis , Lachnospiraceae bacterium GAM79 , Romboutsia ilealis , Faecalibacterium prausnitzii , Roseburia inulinivorans , Roseburia intestinalis , Sarcina sp. JB2 , Uncultured Erysipelotrichaceae bacterium at the species level, was significantly enriched in the control group participants.
note: Clear HC comparison between AD patients and healthy controls

title: The Gut Microbiome in Progressive Multiple Sclerosis
arms: Progressive MS patients vs healthy controls; progressive vs relapsing MS subgroups
quotes: Examining α-diversity, we found no changes in evenness, but found slightly elevated phylogenetic diversity, Shannon diversity, and richness in both RRMS and progressive MS compared to healthy controls (Fig 1A) Examining β-diversity, we found that overall microbiota community structure differed between both progressive and relapsing patients vs. healthy controls but did not differ between progressive and RRMS (Fig 1B,C)

Progressive MS patients shared microbiota alterations with RRMS patients compared to healthy controls, including an increase in Akkermansia at the genus level and Clostridium bolteae at the species level and a decrease in Dorea formicigenerans and unclassified Blautia at the species level.
note: Main HC comparison plus within-disease progressive vs relapsing subgroups

title: Dysbiosis characteristics of gut microbiota in cerebral infarction patients
arms: CI patients vs healthy controls
quotes: At the phylum level, the relative abundance of Firmicutes (50.93% vs 57.55%, FDR = 0.049) and Bacteroidetes (23.53% vs 31.64%, FDR = 0.007) decreased, while Proteobacteria (21.99% vs 9.03%, FDR = 1.09 × 10 ) and Actinobacteria (2.45% vs 0.75%, FDR = 6.26 × 10 ) increased in the CI patients compared with HCs ( Figure 2a ).

The abundances of six BPB, including Faecalibacterium (0.94% vs 7.32%, P < 0.0001), Subdoligranulum (0.35% vs 3.44%, P < 0.0001), Eubacterium rectal group (0.13% vs 0.47%, P < 0.0001), Roseburia (0.12% vs 0.80%, P < 0.0001), Lachnoclostridium (0.11% vs 0.47%, P < 0.0001), and Butyricicoccus (0.10% vs 0.32%, P < 0.0001), decreased significantly in the CI patients ( Figure 2c–h ).
note: Clear HC comparison between CI and healthy controls

title: Differential Patterns of Gut and Oral Microbiomes in Hispanic Individuals with Cognitive Impairment.
arms: Cognitively impaired participants vs cognitively normal controls
quotes: While diversity metrics showed no significant differences between CI and NC groups, differential abundance analysis revealed an increased presence of oral genera such as Dialister , Fretibacterium , and Mycoplasma in CI participants.

Specifically, there was a marked decrease in the relative abundance of Neisseria and an increase in Streptococcus and Fusobacterium in CI participants compared to those who were cognitively normal ( Figure 3 A).
note: HC comparison with both gut and oral microbiota sites

title: Alterations in Gut Microbiota and Their Correlation with Brain Beta-Amyloid Burden Measured by (18)F-Florbetaben PET in Mild Cognitive Impairment Due to Alzheimer's Disease.
arms: Aβ MCI patients vs healthy controls
quotes: Specifically, an increase in the relative abundances of the class Bacilli ( p = 0.034), order Lactobacillales ( p = 0.047), and genus Anaerostipes ( p = 0.036) was noted in the Aβ MCI group.

In this study, we observed a decrease in the abundance of the genera Faecalibacterium [ 22 ], Lachnospira [ 23 ], Oscillibacter [ 24 ], Ruminococcus [ 25 ], Roseburia [ 26 , 27 ], and Alistipes [ 28 ] in the Aβ MCI patients, and this finding is consistent with the findings of previous studies in MCI and AD patients.
note: HC comparison between Aβ MCI and controls

title: Akkermansia muciniphila and its metabolite propionic acid maintains neuronal mitochondrial division and autophagy homeostasis during Alzheimer's disease pathologic process via GPR41 and GPR43.
arms: AD patients vs healthy individuals
quotes: We found that AD patients showed a decrease in the abundance of Akkermansia muciniphila and a decrease in propionic acid both in fecal and in blood.

Absolute quantification of Akkermansia muciniphila levels in AD patients and healthy individuals revealed that Akkermansia muciniphila levels were significantly lower in AD patients than in healthy individuals (Fig. 7 F).
note: Human HC comparison; animal studies used to test mechanism

title: Gut microbiome signatures in iNPH: Insights from a shotgun metagenomics study.
arms: iNPH patients vs healthy controls
quotes: For instance, Enterocloster bolteae displayed a log fold change (lfc) of 6.6 in the iNPH group, compared to 3.7 in the evHC group relative to the nvHC group.

In contrast, enrichment of specific taxa, including Evtepia gabavorous and Cuneatibacter sp. , were specifically associated with iNPH clinical traits, pointing to possible disease-specific microbial markers.
note: HC comparison between iNPH patients and healthy control groups

title: The nasal and gut microbiome in Parkinson's disease and idiopathic rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder.
arms: PD patients vs healthy controls; with/without RBD subgroups
quotes: Eighty percent of the differential gut microbes in PD versus healthy controls showed similar trends in idiopathic rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder, for example, Anaerotruncus and several Bacteroides spp., and correlated with nonmotor symptoms.

Two of the OTUs that were significantly higher abundant in PD compared to HCs ( Akkermansia sp. and Prevotella sp.) were also significantly more highly abundant in PD patients with RBD by PSG compared to PD patients without RBD
note: Main HC comparison; both nasal and gut microbiota; RBD subgroups

title: Primary progressive multiple sclerosis in a Russian cohort: relationship with gut bacterial diversity.
arms: PPMS patients vs healthy controls
quotes: At the class level the relative abundance of Clostridia representatives was lower in the PPMS assemblages (61.2 vs. 63.2%, resp., Fig. 2 a).

However, some PPMS-associated differences were detected in the relative abundance of the rare phyla, i.e. phyla represented by just few OTUs and contributing much less than 1% into the total number of sequences: for example, Verrucomicrobiae with just 4 OTUs showed PPMS-related increase due to Akkermansia muciniphila .
note: HC comparison between PPMS and healthy cohorts using faecal samples

title: Stroke Dysbiosis Index (SDI) in Gut Microbiome Are Associated With Brain Injury and Prognosis of Stroke
arms: Stroke patients vs healthy controls; SDI-H vs SDI-L disease subgroups
quotes: Based on the bacterial 16S rRNA gene data, we identified a total of 18 bacterial genera (FDR_ P < 0.1, Wilcoxon rank-sum test) that were significantly different between patients and controls, with Parabacteroides, Oscillospira , Enterobacteriaceae, etc., enriched in patients, whereas Prevotella, Roseburia, fecalibacterium , etc., were enriched in healthy controls ( Table 2 ).
Patients with higher SDI had increased abundance of Enterobacteriaceae and Parabacteroides and decreased abundance of fecalibacterium , Clostridiaceae, and Lachnospira .
note: Main HC comparison plus SDI-based stroke severity subgroups

title: Relationships Between Rapid Eye Movement Sleep Behavior Disorder and Parkinson's Disease: Indication from Gut Microbiota Alterations.
arms: iRBD/PD with RBD vs normal controls; disease subgroups (iRBD, PD with RBD)
quotes: Enterotype distribution among four groups showed a significant difference (chi-squared, P = 0.004, Fig. 1F-H ), as NC were rich in Bacteroides -dominant enterotype, and they had a lower percentage of Ruminococcus -enriched enterotype.

Furthermore, we focused on the overlapping genera of iRBD vs. NC and PD with RBD vs. NC ( Fig. 2D ), 4 genera ( Aerococcus, Eubacterium , Gordonibacter and Stenotrophomonas ) were found consistently increased while 3 genera ( Butyricicoccus, Faecalibacterium and Haemophilus ) were found consistently decreased in iRBD and PD with RBD group.
note: HC comparison with multiple disease subgroups (iRBD, PD with/without RBD)

title: Spinal cord injury-induced gut dysbiosis influences neurological recovery partly through short-chain fatty acids

arms: MCI/AD patients vs nondementia healthy controls

In contrast, Escherichia-Shigella (p = 0.0002), Bacteroides (p = 0.0014), Holdemanella (p < 0.0001), Romboutsia (p = 0.001), and Megamonas (p = 0.047) were the dominant genera in the AD group.
note: HC comparison between MCI/AD patients and healthy controls in Thai cohort

title: Analysis of gut microbiota in patients with cerebral autosomal dominant arteriopathy with subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopathy (CADASIL)
arms: CADASIL patients vs healthy controls; CADASIL with vs without stroke
quotes: In CADASIL patients compared with controls, there was a significant increase in abundance of 6 genera ( Lachnospira , Odoribacter , Parvimonas , unclassified genus belonging to Barnesiellaceae and Lachnospiraceae , unclassified genus belonging to order SHA-98), and a significant decrease in 2 genera ( Megasphaera and Acidaminococcus ) (Table 2 ).
In the CADASIL patients with compared with those without stroke, there was a significant decrease in abundance of 2 genera, Phascolarctobacterium and Paraprevotella (Table 2 ).
note: Compares disease vs controls and within-disease stroke status subgroups.

title: CXCR3+ T cells in multiple sclerosis correlate with reduced diversity of the gut microbiome.
arms: MS patients vs healthy controls
quotes: Patients exhibited decreased abundance of Coprococcus, Clostridium, and an unidentified Ruminococcaceae genus compared to healthy controls.
note: MS patients compared to healthy controls.

title: Colonic bacterial composition in Parkinson's disease.
arms: Parkinson's disease patients vs healthy controls
quotes: putative, "anti-inflammatory" butyrate-producing bacteria from the genera Blautia, Coprococcus, and Roseburia were significantly more abundant in feces of controls than PD patients.
note: PD patients compared to healthy controls; both stool and mucosal samples mentioned.

title: Comparing the gut microbiome of obese, African American, older adults with and without mild cognitive impairment | PLOS One
arms: Older adults with MCI (cases) vs without MCI (controls)
quotes: Using amplicon 16S rRNA gene sequencing in a case-control study of 60 older (ages 55–76), obese, predominately female, African American adults, those with MCI (cases) had different gut microbiota profiles than controls
note: MCI patients vs healthy controls in obese older adults.

title: Detection of Microbial 16S rRNA Gene in the Blood of Patients With Parkinson's Disease.
arms: PD patients vs healthy controls
quotes: The following genera were enriched in the blood of PD patients: Isoptericola , Cloacibacterium , Enhydrobacter and Microbacterium ; whereas genus Limnobacter was enriched in the healthy controls after adjusting for age, gender, body mass index (BMI) and constipation.
note: PD vs healthy controls, blood microbiota not stool.

title: Distinct gut microbiome characteristics and dynamics in patients with Parkinson's disease based on the presence of premotor rapid-eye movement sleep behavior disorders
arms: PD-RBD(+) vs PD-RBD(-) vs healthy controls (HC)
quotes: In PD-RBD(+), an increased abundance of genera Escherichia (when compared to PD-RBD[−]), Desulfovibrio , Barnesiella , Eisenbergiella (when compared to HC), Akkermansia and Hungatella (when compared to both PD-RBD[−] and HC) was found on shotgun data (Fig. 2 A and B).
note: Compares PD subgroups (with/without RBD) against healthy controls.

title: Gut Microbiome Features of Chinese Patients Newly Diagnosed with Alzheimer's Disease or Mild Cognitive Impairment
arms: AD/MCI patients vs healthy controls
quotes: Patients with AD had decreased Bacteroides, Lachnospira, and Ruminiclostridium_9 and increased Prevotella at the genus level compared with healthy controls.
note: AD and MCI patients compared to healthy controls.

title: Gut dysbiosis and lack of short chain fatty acids in a Chinese cohort of patients with multiple sclerosis.
arms: MS patients vs NMOSD patients
quotes: The gut microbiome of MS patients was characterized by an increase of Streptococcus and a decrease of Prevotella_9; additionally, compared to NMOSD patients, Prevotella_9 was found to be much more abundant in MS patients.
note: Compares one disease (MS) to another disease (NMOSD), not healthy controls.

title: Gut dysbiosis influences the pathophysiology of multiple sclerosis: A case-control study from North India.
arms: MS patients vs healthy controls
quotes: Firmicutes was found to be the most abundant phylum in both groups with significant enrichment in MS than HC.
note: Clear MS vs HC comparison with significant dysbiosis reported.

title: Gut microbiome dysbiosis drives metabolic dysfunction in Familial dysautonomia.
arms: Familial dysautonomia patients vs patient relatives/controls

note: Paired t-test comparing FD patients to relatives with statistical significance.

title: Gut microbiota and metabolome in sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease.
quotes: Several bacteria taxa in sCJD patients were increased at genus level, such as Turicibacter, norank_f_Christensenellaceae, Eisenbergiella, Bilophila and Holdemania.
note: No explicit control arm mentioned in provided sentence.

title: Human gut microbiome gene co-expression network reveals a loss in taxonomic and functional diversity in Parkinson's disease.
arms: PD patients vs healthy controls
quotes: We find that the expression of these genes is decreased in PD compared to HC, especially in genera such as Blautia and Anaerobutyricum but increased in Flavonifractor plautii , a bacterial species that we previously highlighted as associated with HC .
note: Clear PD vs HC comparison with differential gene expression across multiple taxa.

title: Imbalance of Microbacterial Diversity Is Associated with Functional Prognosis of Stroke
arms: Stroke patients vs control subjects
quotes: At the level of phylum, the poststroke subjects showed a significant increase in the relative abundances of Akkermansiaceae , Fusobacteriota , Desulfobacterota, Ruminococcaceae , and Oscillospirales and a particularly noticeable decrease in the relative abundance of Acidobacteriota compared to the control subjects ( P 0.05).
note: Poststroke vs control subjects with statistically significant phylum-level differences.

title: Metaproteogenomic analysis of saliva samples from Parkinson's disease patients with cognitive impairment
arms: PD patients (by cognitive impairment stage) vs healthy controls
quotes: Both metaproteome and microbiota profiles indicated Streptococcus, Prevotella, Veillonella, Fusobacterium and Neisseria as the most abundant bacterial genera in the study cohort which is in agreement with a previous study comparing salivary microbiota of healthy controls and PD patients
note: HC comparison plus CI stratification within PD.

title: Mild cognitive impairment has similar alterations as Alzheimer's disease in gut microbiota.
arms: Alzheimer's disease vs mild cognitive impairment
quotes: Escherichia was observed increased at genus level in both fecal and blood samples from AD and MCI.
note: Compares AD to MCI without healthy control arm in provided sentences.

title: Oral Microbiome Stamp in Alzheimer's Disease
arms: Alzheimer's disease patients vs healthy controls
quotes: We have characterized the bacterial taxonomic composition of the oral microbiome from AD patients (n = 64) compared to the healthy group (n = 71) using 16S ribosomal RNA sequencing
note: AD vs healthy controls with sample sizes and 16S sequencing.

title: Parkinson's disease-associated alterations of the gut microbiome predict disease-relevant changes in metabolic functions
arms: PD cases vs controls
quotes: This odds ratio of 1.8 means that the odds of a certain sequence read being assigned to A. muciniphila was estimated to be 80% higher in PD cases than in controls.
note: PD vs controls with odds ratios for differential abundance.

title: The alteration of gut microbiome and metabolism in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis patients.
arms: ALS patients vs healthy controls
quotes: The analysis of fecal community diversity with 16S rDNA sequencing showed an obvious change in microbial structure of ALS patients, where Bacteroidetes at the phylum level and several microbes at the genus level were up-regulated, while Firmicutes at the phylum level and Megamonas at the genus level were down-regulated compared to healthy controls.
note: ALS vs healthy controls with significant phylum and genus-level changes.

title: The link between increased Desulfovibrio and disease severity in Parkinson's disease.
arms: PD patients (by disease severity) vs healthy controls
quotes: The results showed that Desulfovibrio was significantly increased in PD compared to healthy controls and positively correlated with disease severity.
note: HC comparison plus within-PD severity stratification.

title: The relationship between the gut microbiome and mild cognitive impairment in patients without dementia: a cross-sectional study conducted in Japan.
arms: Mild cognitive impairment vs cognitively normal patients
quotes: In conclusion, an increased prevalence of Bacteroides is independently associated with the presence of MCI in patients without dementia.
note: MCI vs cognitively normal within non-dementia patient population.

title: Unique trans-kingdom microbiome structural and functional signatures predict cognitive decline in older adults.
arms: Alzheimer's disease and mild cognitive impairment vs cognitively healthy controls
quotes: Vogt, et al. showed that Blautia, Phascolarctobacterium, Gemella, Bacteroides, Bilophila , and Alistipes bacteria (many of them are commensal pathogens) were significantly increased, and SMB53 (family Clostridiaceae ), Dialister , Clostridium , Turicibacter , Bifidobacterium, Adlercreutzia , and cc115 (family Erysipelotrichaceae ) (many of them are beneficial/probiotics) were specifically decreased in gut of AD patients compared to controls
note: AD and MCI vs cognitively healthy controls with identified biomarker signatures.
